utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. And I must add, welcome back from your surgery and then other parts. Good afternoon to everyone. May we have the appearances, please. MR. DI FAZIO: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Gramsci Di Fazio, Joanna Korner, and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Ms. Merinda Stewart appearing for the Stanisic Defence this afternoon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Aleksandar Aleksic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm here just to make an application in respect of Witness ST-065. Could we go into private session while I make the application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, while the witness is being brought in, yesterday I showed him a map, 65 ter 3121, but forgot to ask that it be tendered. I apply for it to be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So that may be admitted and marked as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1748, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, sir. Before I invite Mr. Di Fazio to resume his examination-in-chief, I remind you you're still on your oath. Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Examination by Mr. Di Fazio: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to wrap up from yesterday, you -- you said that the -- I think it was Prazina had obtained -- Alija Prazina had obtained a small number of M48s, and of the 150 to 200 men who were doing guard duties, they only had their own personal weapons. Apart from the M48s and their personal weapons, did any villagers have any other weapons of any description whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have now mentioned 150 men being armed, but that is not correct. There were only about two dozen rifles and a good dozen of hunting rifles. That's all the weapons I knew about, which would make a total of about 30 or 35 rifles, which -- part of which were M48, and the others were hunting rifles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. Up until the morning of the 22nd of May, 1992, were you aware of any calls for you and your fellow villagers who were part of this loose defence of the -- of the village being called upon to surrender your weapons? Are you aware of any calls from any quarter, from anywhere, to hand in your weapons?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was only one telephone in all of Renovica, so it wasn't possible to contact us, really. But the only thing I know is that Malko Koroman said that there was some conversation about those rifles. But I wasn't present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you learn that?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was during that period. The war broke out on the 4th in Sarajevo, and until the 20th - I'm not sure of the exact date. It may have been about two weeks before Renovica was attacked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you're aware, had there been any arrangements made for you and your fellow villagers to surrender your weapons?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Now turn your mind to the 22nd of May, 1992. At the time, were you still residing in Renovica?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the evening of the 21st to the 22nd, what had you been doing during the night?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That night, with my neighbours and relatives - I don't know if their names matter to you - we went out to guard the village. But that group of ours only had one M48 rifle. And we were on guard behind our houses. I could describe the exact spot to you, but I don't know if it would mean much to you. It's called Cetici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks, that's all I needed to know. Did the night pass uneventfully and did you eventually go to bed in the morning of the 22nd of May in 1992?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. It was a beautiful May night, and the other guys went to sleep about 2.00. And I remained there with my uncle, Esad Hujdur, until 5.00 or quarter after 5.00. And there was -- and then a bus passed by, a bus of the Centar Trans company. It still ran on that road. And once the bus passed, then we both also went to sleep to our respective houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you now tell the Trial Chamber how you awoke, what woke you, and describe events.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that night, Mr. Rasim Suceska also slept in my house. He was a lad and it was just after the month of Ramadan. He was studying to become a Muslim priest, but he couldn't go back to Sarajevo because the war had started there in the meantime, and he spent the night in my house, just as did my father and mother. And I came back around quarter after 5.00 and went to bed, and I was aroused by some shooting but I didn't get up immediately. And then my mother entered the room and said, Get up, kids, there are soldiers outside. And I put on a track suit and some socks and I tried to get out of the house. But as soon as I peeped out the door, my gaze went right and on the cross-roads, at the cross-roads where my house is, there was a Pinzgauer vehicle with a machine-gun mounted. And they were shooting from that machine-gun at the roofs of the houses in the village of Turkovici. I was scared, and went back to the house immediately. And my mother also insisted that we return. And you could hear bullets flying. One bullet flew through our window into our house. And she called us to come to the hallway because it was a sort of shelter; there were no windows there. And we stayed there maybe ten minutes or so. We were lying down and all the while there was shooting outside. The hallway -- from the hallway there is also a door to the bathroom. And the door was open, and I could see part of the village. Some houses were already burning. Some -- we lay there about ten minutes and somebody was calling from a megaphone, was calling out to all people to come out and surrender their weapons but nobody dared come out. After this appeal from the megaphone, the firing resumed. I'm not sure what kind of weapons they used. Probably automatic rifles. And for some ten or 15 minutes, but I'm not sure about the exact duration, there was shooting. Then it subsided again and stopped. After some five or ten minutes, I'm not sure, Reuf Jusic, a neighbour, came to the door and he called at my father, Father, come out. Our police from Pale has come to check if we have weapons. They won't harm us. I don't know if this is enough for the time being?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. It's a good start. Can you tell us, during the events that you've just described, right up until the time the man came and called out to your father, did you return fire? Or did anyone in your house offer any resistance?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Resistance couldn't be offered from my house because I didn't have any weapons. Nobody in my house had any weapons, so we couldn't open fire, nor was anybody present expect for myself, my father, Rasim Suceska, and my mother.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now the man came and called to your father, called for surrender. Did you and your family surrender yourselves?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: My father went out first, and my mother, and then myself and Rasim Suceska. Once we stepped out, five to ten men were standing there pointing their rifles at us. As soon as we appeared in front of the house, they ordered us to put our hands up, which we did. They said, Hands up, and one of them or two, I'm not sure, approached us and searched us. And at the same moment, a number of them entered the house. I don't know what they did there because we were outside. After that search, they took us to -- toward the house of Pasija Milic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you eventually arrive at Milic's house?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were four of us, one behind the other. And that house is about a hundred metres from mine. In the basement and on the ground floor there were already neighbours of mine. Five or six people were standing in front of that house. They were dressed in camouflage uniforms and in reserve police uniforms. My father recognised some people and some even greeted him. We were all put in the basement or in the ground -- or on the ground floor of that house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thinking back, how many people were in the house when you first arrived, and did the numbers increase during the course of the day?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot be certain, but ten, 15, or 20 people were detained in that house when we were there. After some time, a man ordered Velija Hujdur and Reuf Jusic to go and tell the other neighbours to surrender. Or else, since Velija Hujdur's daughter and Jusic's son were already there, they would. If they didn't -- didn't return, they would shoot their children. And I think they came back and brought Ramiz Hujdur to that basement. And, again, I'm not sure of the exact number but there were maybe 20 or 25 people there in all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All villagers of Renovica and the surrounding hamlets?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What I've described so far, first we were taken from Turkovici to that place. And after a time that we spent in Pasija Milic's house, they would take us to the military apartments at Renovica. We spent about an hour in the basement of that house, and all us, 25 or 30 - I'm really not sure of the exact number - we were taken to Renovica, which is about 300 to 400 metres away, where there were military apartments where the officers of the former JNA used to live. Once we were brought to that building and into one of those apartments, we found people from the surrounding villages, Petovici, Vinca, Lunje, and there were about 40 or 50 people there. But, again, I'm not sure about the exact numbers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Men, women, and children?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Men, women, children, and elderly folks; everybody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks for giving us that description. Now I want you to go back to the period of time when you first came out of your house and surrendered to the period of time when you ended up in Milic's house. So far you've described one Pinzgauer that was firing. On that day, did you see any other Pinzgauers? Was it just one or were there more?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment, or, rather, while they were taking us there, there was constant shooting at Renovica, and barns were burning. The Pinzgauer was still standing there when we were coming back, and the column was at least a kilometre long. I was able to conclude that they had arrived with a greater number of vehicles and many weapons. But they deployed. So one group went to Turkovici, one group to Renovica, the -- another to Petovici, because they attacked all villages at once. One group went to Kaljani; one went to Lunje. And once we set off in the direction of Pale, I noticed that the column was about a kilometre long.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, column -- column of what? Column of villagers or column of vehicles, of -- of Pinzgauers? What are you talking about here?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the column of military vehicles. Pinzgauers, Pragas, and there were also two buses full of soldiers where they put also the prisoners and -- who they took toward Pale. That's the column I mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. We'll get to those events in just a while. In the meantime, I want to focus on the -- again, on the period of time --

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The period of time when you come out of your house and before you get to the Milic house. That period of time. You've told us about the Pinzgauers. What about the men who were there, these men who were involved in this -- in this episode? Were they dressed in uniform?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, they all were. But I may have left out that at the entrance to Pasija Milic's house there were about five to ten soldiers. I'm again not sure about the exact number. They were all dressed in camouflage uniforms and reserve police uniforms. And I can tell because I lived there and they patrolled all the time. The uniform did differ from military uniforms. The colour of the uniform was blue, which -- by which I can tell that they were reserve police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember - if you can't, that's fine - but if you can remember, can you tell us how many or approximately how many reserve police uniforms you saw that morning when you first came out to surrender?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't quite understand the question. The number of uniforms or the number of men?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry. Yeah, that's my fault. What I meant was the number of men dressed in reserve police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the outset, by my house, around ten and another ten down at Renovica. But when we left Pasija Milic's house toward Renovica, toward the military apartments, we were in a group, and the soldiers were -- walked with us. My father and I were ordered to carry a box of ammunition. And with that group of ours that went toward Renovica, there must have been 20, 25, or 30 of them. But I cannot be sure of the exact number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Think back. Were they all soldiers? Were any of them policemen?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were policemen. My conclusion was that half of them were police officers, because they all wore reserve police uniforms, and they were probably all police officers. But the people wearing camouflage uniforms, not all their uniforms were green. Some were blue and white, like police uniforms. On that day, I saw these three kinds of uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And the -- can you tell us, if you know, the ethnicity of the men who wore uniforms and who participated in the attack?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know all those men, but I can mention one man whom I recognised. Zeljko Cvoro. He was an acquaintance of mine. I was a sportist and that's how I know him. And I know that his name is Zeljko Cvoro, but I didn't know the rest of them. Talking about the group that was taking us to the military apartment at Renovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you got any idea what Zeljko's Cvoro's job was back then in 1992, who he worked with, or ...

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he was a waiter in a pub at Praca. But he was a member of the reserve police, because at that time everybody was drafted either to the army or to the reserve police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You've told us about being taken to the Milic house and then from there to the barracks, the Renovica barracks; correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not to the barracks. To the apartments where the officers of the former JNA lived. Those were their apartments. But apartments built for military personnel at Renovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. And thanks for that clarification. And were they close to the barracks or part of the barracks system?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they weren't part of the barracks system. They about 300 or 400 metres from the barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's not in -- we know that you eventually were taken to Pale, or at least that's what -- the evidence we expect. But what I'm interested in is the period of time in this -- these apartments. While you were being held there, approximately how many villagers would you say eventually were gathered up into those apartments?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have skipped a detail. When we were walking from Pasija Milic's house to the military apartments, in my statement I mentioned that in front of those apartments there were more soldiers, and later we concluded that their headquarters was there and that they actually managed the attack on Renovica from there. In front of those apartments we saw another ten or 20 soldiers, and that's where I first saw Radomir Kojic. When we were approaching that house, one of the police officers who was also dressed in a reserve police uniform came up to me, and I mentioned already that my father and I were carrying a box of ammunition because we were ordered to do so, and he asked me, Balija, where is your rifle? And hit me in the face. After that, we were taken into the apartment, and there I saw 50 to 60 persons. It was a two-room apartment, and it was full of people. They were sitting on the floor and so there may have been 50 or 60 of them. I don't know if this is enough for you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Just one detail I want to clarify. You said that you -- when you got to the front of the apartments you saw another 10 or 20 soldiers. All I want to be clear about is - doing the best you can and thinking back - tell us this: Were they soldiers or policemen? If they were soldiers, that's fine. But I just want to know how exactly they were dressed or what exactly -- which organisation they were members of.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it was more likely that they belonged to police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now can you -- do you have any basis for saying that? I'm talking about the ten or 20 that you saw in front of the apartments. Do you have any basis for saying that?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only base that I can have, that I can conclude about, is that those people who were there, as I have told you, wore the reserve police uniforms. They had camouflage uniforms as well, and blue camouflage uniforms. The ones I used to see special MUP units wear before. So that was the only basis for me making this conclusion that they belonged to police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you described being gathered in the -- the apartments, the officers' apartments, 50 or 60 of you. And how long were you there for?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We stayed there -- let me see. The attack started at 8.00 and we stayed there perhaps until 4.00 or 4.30. And I don't know if you're interested in this detail, but at around 2.00, approximately, they released the elderly, women, and children, including my father, and they kept some 30 of us there. So we could have stayed there until 4.00 or 4.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who did they keep? Just the men?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only the men. That is to say, just us. The men were kept in that room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Describe now how you came to leave the room, how you came to leave Renovica, and how you got to Pale.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most likely some of the people who were in command of that unit ordered for us to get up. A guy approached us, told to us put our hands up in the air so they could tie our hands with a rope, and they ordered us to move toward the bus. All of us were boarded on the bus, and there could have been 25 to 30 of us there. I think the exact number was 26, that 26 men were taken from Renovica to Pale. The soldiers got on the same bus, that is to say that we were on the same bus with the soldiers. And then the column was established. And as I have said earlier, that column was about one kilometre long. There were at least three Pragas there, Pinzgauers, trucks, 110 trucks, and this is how I am able to tell you that the column was about one kilometre long. So we got on the bus and the column started moving towards Pale. Then the column stopped in front of the house of Prazina Alija. The second or third vehicle behind us stopped in front of that house and they started firing on the house and basically it was bullet-ridden after that. Then we continued our trip to Pale. As for the people on the bus with us, reserve police forces and so on, we talked to them and it had an encouraging tone, the conversation. They kept telling us that we were going to Pale, that they wanted to interview us there, and this is how we arrived to Pale where some 200 to 300 people awaited us. There were civilians there and ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Just -- just -- I realize there's just one more detail I want to get before we get to events at Pale. Earlier in your evidence you described some of the dwellings in your hamlet of Turkovici burning. Can you give the Trial Chamber an idea of how many buildings you saw burning or being destroyed by fire and when you saw that.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the very outset, in the morning, I can claim with certainty that in my immediate neighbourhood two stables were set on fire and one or two houses. Esad Hujrija's [phoen] house and perhaps another house. As we were transported from Milic, Pasija's house to the military apartments, I can't give you the exact number but we saw a lot of houses burning. At least a dozen houses were on fire in the neighbourhood. Hujdur, Alija's house, stable, and so on. I passed by his house and this is how I know for a fact it was on fire. Safet's stable was also on fire. And I saw all this. This is how I'm able to claim this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And lastly, on -- on -- still dealing with Renovica, you describe being struck or hit once. Do you know if any other prisoners were assaulted in any way? Now -- I'm talking now back at Renovica and in the surrounding hamlets.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you anything about the surrounding hamlets. As for Renovica itself, before going into the apartment, I saw that Kasim Sipovic was being beaten at the very down-town of Renovica. At the main intersection there he was being beaten by young men. I don't know why. So when Kasim was brought to that apartment, he was already all bloody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. And I'm sorry to interrupt your narrative. Now, go back to the point where you arrive in the convoy in Pale. Where exactly in Pale were you taken?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Pale, the column stopped in front of the MUP building. That's how we referred to that building. This is where over 200 people awaited us. I can't give you the exact number, but there were civilians there and people wearing reserve police uniforms. There were soldiers. And there were over 200 of them altogether in that group. They ordered us to get off the bus. And as we were entering the MUP building, they told us to stand up against the wall. And in the meantime they started swearing at us, Balijas, you killed one of our men. All of them need to be shot. And then this mob moved toward us to beat us. As they started beating us, I was hit a couple of times. There were two or three of them to each one of us when they were beating us. After some time, somebody ordered - most likely Malko Koroman - to take us to the culture hall, which is a sports hall nowadays. There was a gauntlet that they established, and we walked in pairs through the gauntlet towards the building. And as we walked, they hit us whenever they could. When we entered the old culture hall, or the sports hall nowadays, we saw some 15 to 20 people there who had been imprisoned before us. This mob that beat us in front of the MUP building and in that gauntlet entered the building as well and continued beating us. I described this in my first statement. And there was a man - I'm not sure about his name, but it could be Guja, Radomir - who wore the uniform of a reserve policeman. He beat the daughter of Sevko Suljevic with a table leg. Sevko fell to the ground. And back in -- in my 1992 statement I described how he beat him directly on the head. So this beating continued for some ten to 15 minutes after they brought us into the building, and then Malko Koroman showed up and he ordered them to leave the premises of the old culture hall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Just a few more details about this. The mob that menaced you and tried to attack you, who -- who made up the mob?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will repeat once again. When we came up there, there were civilians waiting for us there, as well as men in the former JNA uniforms; also men wearing reserve police uniforms and camouflage uniforms which were blue/grey. I suppose these were some special MUP units. There were also people wearing green camouflage uniforms. This group numbered over 200 people. I don't know if this is sufficient for you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of the policemen who were present, reserve policemen or otherwise, do anything to protect you?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember anything except for the entrance of Malko Koroman, who came in after they beat us. He came into the old culture hall and in a strict voice he ordered them to leave. So the only person who intervened was Malko Koroman, who ordered them to leave the premises.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you imprisoned at the culture hall near the Pale SJB? For what period of time?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: 50 days. After that time, we were transferred to Kula and remained there for another 50 days. I was exchanged after being in prison for 100 days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you were in the -- in the culture centre in Pale during the period of your imprisonment, who guarded you? Who secured the place?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the very entrance there was always a guard wearing a reserve police uniform. I knew one of them personally because he used to play football with me. His name is Savic. I also knew another guard who was a teacher in our place. I think his last name was Bosovic. Both of them wore reserve police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Were you and your fellow prisoners beaten during the time that you were imprisoned?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we were imprisoned there, four men died as a result of beatings. They were beaten brutally. I can give you the names. Nasko Smajic was beaten and died as a result. Edhem Hrvo, as well, died under shady circumstances. Selim Pandzic was also beaten brutally in front of my eyes by allegedly special police units from Pale. And actually that was a unit under the command of Rajko Kusic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Anyone commit suicide?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for Edhem Hrvo, I can't claim with certainty how he died. He died down there. I don't know how he died, whether he committed suicide or he succumbed to the injuries he received during the beating. I'm not sure. As for the two men Pandzic and Smajic, I can assure you that they were brutally beaten and died as a result.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Sorry, would Your Honours just bear with me for a moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You touched upon this earlier -- not -- not long ago you mentioned that I think when you were being threatened by the crowd, or mob, that you were being blamed or connected somehow with the death of some Serb men at Renovica that day. Do you know who was killed? Which Serb men were killed, if any, at Renovica on that day, the 22nd of May?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among the people that were with us on the bus, the reserve policemen, soldiers, and so on, as I have described to you, we heard from them that, allegedly, a tenant [as interpreted] was killed and somebody else. That's what we heard while on the bus. I don't know whether this is true. We had no contact with anybody ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, 20 -- page 20, line 2, it's recorded as tenant, which is the -- which is the translation of the surname -- the exact translation of the surname of that person. But I think it's -- his surname is Stanar. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm grateful for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let just go back. What I'm asking you about is not you or your fellow villagers but any of the Serb men who came to Renovica that day, the 22nd of May. Were any of them killed?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: You probably misunderstood me. Those two Serbs that the men on the bus mentioned had allegedly died, had been allegedly killed. Their names were Stanar and another man. I'm now referring to the people who came to Renovica on that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how they were killed, if they were killed?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I truly don't know. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And were any of your fellow villagers from Turkovici, Renovica, or the surrounding hamlets killed on that day? I'm talking about there, at Renovica or -- or the hamlets, not in Pale.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, nobody was killed on that day, but they were wounded. Milic, Sipovic, Munib Salispahic [phoen]. And then Cutuk as well; I don't know his first name. The three of them were wounded on that day. It was at the very beginning when they opened fire. As the residents were fleeing towards the forest, they opened fire, and three people were wounded on that day. MR. DI FAZIO: Can the witness be shown P1450. It's a photograph. And can I ask for the usher's assistance in asking the witness to mark the screen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I want you to look at this photograph and I'm going to ask you some questions about it. And the usher will help you. You can actually mark the screen with a special pen that he'll give you. What I want you to do is to see if you can see in that photograph the Pale SJB building. If you can, circle it.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's this building here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Only touch the screen when told to, please. Can you see ...

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no, that's fine. Perfect. Thank you. Can you see the place, is it visible, this place that you've referred to as the culture centre?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I? May I circle it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead and circle it.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I seek to tender that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1749, Your Honours. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hujdur, thank you very much for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hujdur, we just have one, perhaps two, questions at the most. You spoke about the preparations for defence, as you called them, in Renovica. Within those preparations, some of the residents of Renovica went to Croatia for training; right?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You also were invited to go to Croatia; right?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not invited. I was told this verbally. The Defence teams probably know that I was into sports. I was a sportsman, an athlete. And allegedly seven of us from Renovica were supposed to go to this training in Croatia. And out of seven, only two went.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Asko Prazina and Fadil Sifovic [phoen] went; right?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Asko Prazina, is --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Is it the same person as Alija?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the son of the late Alija.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did they all come back?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did they tell you what this training in Croatia comprised?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw Asko after the training. He lived in Sarajevo. As for Fadil Sifovic, he and I were never on good terms. So I never got in touch with him, and he never told me anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You didn't go to this training because you had work obligation to perform; right?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had work obligation to perform, and I was also an athlete during that period of time. I was a football player, and I attended football training and preparations in Ucina.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'm following your statement. And in the statement you gave to the OTP, you claim that you had work obligation. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did have work obligation. But at the same time, I went to Ucina for soccer, for football training.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Since you have been a member of the SDA since 1991, do you know that the SDA sent its members to Croatia for training to become policemen, members of specialist forces. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, you can check my files. I was a football player. And I did become a member of the SDA but nothing more than a member. I did vote in elections for the SDA; but other than that, I never attended any meetings nor do I know about these people going for training. You can check this for yourself. You can check all my files, and you'll see that I'm telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'm just asking you to receive an answer from you. You don't have to be concerned about my questions.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there's a village called Bare where a family of ten was killed, a family called Vukasinovic, men, women, children. Do you know about this incident?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know these place called Bare. However, these people were not killed during that period of time. They were killed after we had been imprisoned in Pale. It could have been in early June or late May, because we heard it while in prison. It didn't happen while we were free.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And I am putting it to you that this was in early April 1992. It is possible that you heard about this later. Would you allow for this possibility?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This was in my neighbourhood after all. And during that period of time, in Renovica -- in Renovica and in Bare, there was not a single murder. I can assure you of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. At the very end, something that we typically see with witnesses and I will tell you about it. I have a statement that gave to the Sarajevo SJB, the State Security Department. You remember giving this statement on the 30th of August, 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As soon as I left the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: For the Trial Chamber, the ERN number is 0021-6896. And the last ERN number is 0021-6900.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Is it on the document list, Mr. Cvijetic? No?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. And I will not use it -- I will not ask that it be tendered into evidence. I will just use it to put questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm comparing this to the statement you gave. In that statement, you say that there were policemen there and the first time that you saw them was when you arrived in front of the MUP building and up until that time you only saw one sort of uniforms. Whereas today you seem to say that you had seen a number of different uniforms. Why this discrepancy?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I don't know whether you know about the condition in which we left the prison. Your Honours, we left the camp on the 28th and this is when we were exchanged. I gave the statement on the 30th. Most likely I skipped a number of items in that statement. And as for these uniforms, believe me, you don't need to rely just on me. Any resident of Renovica can confirm this to you. There were different uniforms there. There was a diversity of uniforms. There were camouflage uniforms, blue/grey. There were reserve police uniforms, military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. So it is your position that the statement that you gave, when you arrived on the Muslim territory, is not entirely true; right?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, everything there is true. But perhaps I did not go into great details in that statement. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I'm not objecting, but I -- just in order to be able to follow this evidence, I need to know where in the statement the witness said that when he arrived in front of the MUP and up until that time he had only seen one sort of uniform. I can't find that in the statement. If Mr. Cvijetic would be so kind as to direct me to it, then I can ... I can sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, you misunderstood my words.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I said that if we read the statement and reach the section where you come in front of the MUP building and you mentioned a Pinzgauer there, which is on page 2 of your statement, that there were about a dozen soldiers in camouflage uniforms. And you go on to say - that's on page 4 - that a soldier in camouflage uniform kicked you in the belly. Correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He did that when I came to Pale, when I was taken to the MUP building allegedly to make a statement. And when the guy was taking me from the former cultural centre to the MUP building, some youngster kicked me in the belly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But your statement says a soldier. That's why I'm asking. Is it correct that it was a soldier who did it?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... okay, I -- it doesn't matter all that much to me. But speaking about that particular incident, you said that an acquaintance protected you and that you were not mistreated while you were giving a statement in the MUP building and when you left the MUP building. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm really here to -- just to say the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did -- did he protect you? Just say that.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did. But I still don't know who he is. But I'm -- I am grateful to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You failed to say today that you were later taken to Kula which was an official prison.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: After 50 days in prison, we were taken to Kula.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You said that you were treated fairly there and that you even had four meals a day when you had to work physically; correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Furthermore you spoke about this special unit of sorts. But I see that this unit was led by one Slavica Jovanovic, a woman. That's what you say.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slavica Jovanovic brought those guys. But it was our conclusion later that Rajko Kusic actually was the leader of the unit. They were Rajko Kusic's men.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And you say you've heard that he also wore a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He also had some sort -- I cannot state with any certainty though.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: We are speaking about Slavica Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Slavica Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You cannot be sure who she belonged to?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: She mostly came with that group. I don't know if you want to know the names of the people I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'm only interested in her.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was always came with that group that belonged to Rajko Kusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: It has been pointed out to me that one cannot tell from the transcript that we're speaking about a woman.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, about a woman.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you were speaking about a woman. Was that woman wearing a uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, she was dressed in a uniform. I have been speaking about uniforms a lot. There were three or four kinds of uniforms. The people who came to the prison on the occasion of the attack on us and everything else, there were uniforms of the reserve police which I know well. They have this characteristic blue/grey pattern. Then there were green camouflage uniforms. Then there were blue and grey uniforms, which makes me think that they were police officers. I really can't be sure about Slavica Jovanovic. I think that she wore some sort of an overall. Whether it was blue/grey or green/grey, I'm not sure now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And when you speak in general about soldiers or a soldier, what kind of uniform can they wear, in your opinion? When you're talking about a soldier, what uniform do they wear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I also served in the former JNA, so I was a soldier of that army. And the regular uniform of a JNA soldier is green. And I never saw camouflage uniforms until the war. While I was serving in the JNA, the uniforms were plain green, actually olive-drab, if we're speaking about soldiers, proper soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So in -- proper soldiers as you say. So in what you were telling us today, when you speak about soldiers, you speak about military men? You mean military men. Not men in blue uniforms, not men in police uniforms. For instance, the man who kicked you in the belly was a military man, because in your statement, you said: "Soldier."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that he was a soldier. He probably was. I -- I really don't know. I was being taken from the room where we were detained to the MUP building and then a man dressed as a soldier kicked me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Is there cross-examination on ... on behalf of -- of the Zupljanin Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, we don't have a question for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have anything in re-examination, Mr. -- MR. DI FAZIO: Just two very brief matters. Re-examination by Mr. Di Fazio:

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In your statement given on the 30th of August, 1992, to the Security Services Centre Sarajevo, did you say -- I can show it to you if you wish, but if you have any memory tell us, when describing the military -- you were going into the military apartment building, did you say this, or words to this effect: "We formed a column, and the aggressors's soldiers mixed among us because they were afraid of sniper fire. As I entered" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Where are you quoting from? MR. DI FAZIO: I'm sorry. If Your Honours please, page 3. Page 3, first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: "As I entered a military building, a reserve policeman whose name I do not know hit me in the head in front of my parents" --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I understood Mr. Cvijetic was not -- didn't want to quote from the statement. We cannot follow the statement -- or the accused, actually, cannot follow the statement on the monitor because it -- it's not on the 65 ter list or uploaded in the transcript -- in -- in the e-court. I'm sorry. MR. DI FAZIO: It's 65 ter 9145.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. MR. DI FAZIO: And if we can -- if everyone would prefer me to put it on the screen, I'll do that if that -- I was trying to save time, but I think that, given the circumstances, it's best if we put it up on the screen. So can we have that up on the screen, please. And the B/C/S version as well so -- for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I don't know exactly where this portion is in the B/C/S. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, and Defence counsel are pleased, it's page 3 of the English. So if we can go to page 3 of the English, it's at the top. Right. And I think it would have to be into the next page of the B/C/S at least, and it appears to be at the beginning of the paragraph. So could we go to page 2 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may help. On the following page, the last paragraph. The following page of the B/C/S. MR. DI FAZIO: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Toward the end of the page -- or, actually, the bottom. This is not in dispute. The witness said as much while he was answering your questions today. I'm not sure whether it is really necessary to quote that. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. I'll just wrap this up. In the last paragraph that you can see there in the B/C/S, you should find words to the effect that I was quoting to you. You were talking about forming a column, aggressors' soldiers being mixed up amongst you because of fear of sniper fire, entering a military apartment building, and being hit in the head by a reserve policeman. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see now. And that's what the statement says. But we seem to be mixing things up, the kick I received at Pale and the hit I received here. What is referred to here happened at Renovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness is right. If this is what you're looking for, then -- I mean the incident with the soldier and the kick, that's on page 4. The witness is right. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, he is. But what I'm concerned about is a suggestion that it was only a failure to mention policemen at all until they got to Pale. That's what I'm concerned about. And it's here in the statement. I think I've made my point, and I don't need to go any further with this at this point. So thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You do see the part in the B/C/S where you say - still talking about Renovica, not Pale, Renovica - where you say: "A reserve policeman whose name I do not know hit me in the head in front of my parents." You see that?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I've done with that. And the last issue I want to ask you about just very quickly. You were asked by Defence counsel about a family from Bare, I think, who were killed. At any time on the 22nd of May or in the time that you were in the Pale culture centre imprisoned, did any official or guard, or did you find out from any other source if your predicament, your situation being imprisoned there, was somehow contacted with Bare, what had happened at Bare?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, I can only repeat that the incident at Bare couldn't have happened before the 22nd. I don't know what happened after the 22nd. But I can say for certain that after some time spent at Pale, I'm not sure I -- I'll -- I remember the name of the persons killed correctly. I think it's Vukasinovic. But I know that Vukasinovic guy from sight and my -- because my father was a bus driver, and the father of the Vukasinovic family was on good terms with my father.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I don't want to go into the ins and outs of -- it's a simple question. In the time on 22nd of May or in Pale, when you were imprisoned in Pale, did anyone, a guard, security, other prisoners, anyone, ever suggest to you or say to you that your situation, the fact of being taken from your home and imprisoned, was connected somehow with what had happened in Bare?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... thank you, I --

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I obviously misunderstood. No, that wasn't the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, the witness was interrupted in the middle of his answer on 32 -- page 32, 10. He was explaining that some member of Vukasinovic family came, so -- and then he was interrupted. I would really appreciate if he could finish his -- his answer in full. MR. DI FAZIO: If I interrupted, then I apologise and I shouldn't have.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And, Witness, is there anything further that you wanted to add when you were taking about the Vukasinovic family and when I interrupted you?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL HUJDUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it's interesting to you, Your Honours, I can continue the story. My father and Mr. Vukasinovic -- well, my father was a bus driver and he hung out with Serbs a lot, and he was well respected by people. And when that Mr. Vukasinovic came to the camp or the prison at the culture centre at Pale - he must have been the son of the people killed up there - he came to take it out on us. He really didn't beat me. Whether it was owing to my father, I don't know. But on that day, he came. He brutally beat up Hajrudin Karic. And when I say "he," I mean Mr. Vukasinovic. If you're interested in anything else, ask me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. We thank you for your assistance to the Tribunal, sir. You are now released as a witness, and we wish you a safe journey back to your home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, this brings us conveniently to the ordinary time for the break. I assume your next witness, your next scheduled witness, is ready to come on? MR. DI FAZIO: I believe that is so. And I have been asked to -- yes, that is so. And if we take the adjournment now, that will really serve -- assist us in getting that witness ready and producing him immediately after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we return in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Now, for the Prosecution, I'm Tom Hannis, along with Belinda Pidwell, Selma Sakic, and Crispian Smith. Our next witness is Manojlo Milovanovic, ST-260. He has no protective measures. He is testifying openly, and we're ready to start with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, sir. I would first of all ask you to read the solemn declaration on the card that the usher has handed to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. And from your responses so far, I take it that you are hearing me in a language that you understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I would first of all point out to you that the solemn declaration that you have just made imposes upon you an obligation to speak the truth, under pain of the penalties for perjury which this Tribunal is empowered by its Statute to impose on witnesses who give false or misleading testimony. Welcome to the Tribunal. And you have been called as a witness by the Prosecution. Could you, first of all, tell us your name, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Manojlo Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: What is your date of birth, what is your ethnicity --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 21st of November, 1943. I'm a Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... and what is or was your --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think we had interpretation of your last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cvijetic. Are you hearing me now, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: What is or was your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was a general, lieutenant general, in the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: colonel general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Have you testified previously before this Tribunal or before any of the courts in any of the countries that comprise the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the third time I'm testifying before this Court. I also testified once before the War Crimes Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. I need then only remind you of the procedure that is followed here, that is, that the side calling you begins. The side opposite would have an opportunity to ask questions of you. The side calling then wraps up. And, at that stage, or indeed at any earlier stage, the Bench may have questions of you. The -- your appearance before the Tribunal is in its afternoon sittings, because we share the courtroom space with other trials, and it is expected that your testimony would not be completed today but would in fact extend into tomorrow. We would rise for the day at 7.00 and resume tomorrow afternoon at 2.15. The sessions for each day's sitting are divided into intervals of 90 minutes each and that is primarily to allow for the tapes that record the proceedings to be changed, but it also allows for the convenience of the witnesses, counsel, the Bench, and -- and the support staff to have a break. Those breaks are of 20 minutes' duration. But notwithstanding those set breaks that I have indicated, if at any time during your testimony you have a need for a break, we will, of course, accommodate you. The Prosecution has indicated that they expect that their examination of you would last for three hours. And counsel for the Accused Stanisic has indicated an hour for cross-examination. And counsel for the Accused Zupljanin has indicated an hour and a half. And I would now invite Mr. Hannis, for the Prosecution, to begin. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. I understand that you were a professional soldier. Can you tell us how many years you served in that capacity?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: If we count the schooling I had, I spent a total of 42 years in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what year that career began.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In 1959, I enrolled into the school for non-commissioned officers. I graduated in 1961. Then I worked as non-commissioned officer in Benkovac garrison, near Zadar, for 14 months. Following that, I went to the Military Academy in Belgrade; it lasted for four years. And I graduated in 1966. After that, I served in Banja Luka. Up until 1975, I was a platoon commander, company commander, and I was head of the School of Reserve Officers for Armoured Units. In 1975, I went to the higher Military Academy, as it was known at the time. It was the Command Staff School for Tactics. I graduated in 1977 and went to serve to Prilep garrison where I served as battalion commander for four years. In 1981 I moved to the Titov Veles garrison, where I served as an operative in the motorised brigade. From there I went to the War School in 1986. I graduated the following year, in 1987. And then I returned to the garrison in Titov Veles, where I served as commander of the 212th Motorised Brigade. I remained brigade commander until the 30th of January, 1989, when I was transferred to the command of the 3rd Military District in Skopje as an operative in the army command. I remained there until the 3rd of March, 1992, when I withdrew the combat part of the JNA from Macedonia to Serbia, to the command of the Nis garrison. I remained in Nis until the 11th of May, 1992, when I was transferred to the Sarajevo garrison, to the same post I held in Nis. However, I never reached Sarajevo. I reached as far as the Han Pijesak, near Crna Rijeka, because the command of the 2nd Military District withdrew from Sarajevo on the 3rd of May, after the events in Dobrovoljacka Street. From the 11th of May until the end of the war, I was Chief of Staff of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska and deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. General, can you tell me, what rank did you hold in early 1992 when you were in Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: While in Macedonia, I was a colonel. Upon withdrawal of the JNA from Macedonia, I was given a decree dated the 25th/26th of April, 1992, promoting me to major-general. That is to say, that I arrived in Bosnia as major-general in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how was it that you were sent to Bosnia in 1992? Upon whose -- whose order or whose decree?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 8th of May, 1992. I found myself in the Pec garrison when I was touring the units that had withdrawn from Macedonia. I was told then to return immediately, urgently, to Nis. I arrived there and I was given two presidential decrees. The one on promoting me into major-general, and the second one on my transfer. The presidential decrees were signed by the rump Presidency of the SFRY. The second presidential decree transferred me to the command of the 2nd Military District, Sarajevo garrison, as chief of the operations and training organ, the same position I held in Nis. The decree was to be implemented by the 11th of May. I set out from Nis and I was first supposed to report to the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia to pick up the transfer documents, and I was then told that the first presidential decree on transfer was being changed and that my new position was Chief of Staff of the army. In addition to that, I was given another order; namely, that the JNA was to withdraw from Bosnia by 19th of May, inclusive of the same year. This confused me. I couldn't understand why I was being transferred to the position of the chief of the 2nd Military District if the JNA was to withdraw from Bosnia, because there was a prior agreement between the Presidency of the JNA and the Presidency of Bosnia about the JNA remaining in Bosnia for the -- for another five years to protect equally the interests of all three nations in Bosnia. The chief of the personnel administration of the General Staff, General Gojko Krstic, told me that I would be given more detailed explanations by General Ratko Mladic once I see him in Bosnia. We met in the afternoon in Bosnia, and Mladic explained to me that given that the JNA was to withdraw, the remaining two nations in Bosnia, that is to say, Muslims and Croats, already had their armies, and as a result of that, the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina decided to establish the Army of the Serbian Republic and that we were to remain in that army if we wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you a couple of questions and then we'll return to May of 1992. How -- what year did you retire from the army?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I retired pursuant to my own request, and I received my first pension on the 1st of May, 2001. That is to say, that I did it sometime in March of 2001 after being removed from the position of the minister of defence of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And since that time, have you been fully retired, or have you done other work?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I've been mostly retired since that time. However, for my own needs, I conducted some analyses of the war. I also cooperated with the editorial board of the Academy of Arts and Sciences of Serbia in drafting their encyclopedia. And I have also served as the Republika Srpska senator since --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir, the interpreter did get the last part of your answer. You said you had served as a Republika Srpska senator since ... and we didn't catch the time, the year.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Since May 2009. And my term is for five years unless I'm removed due to some errors I may commit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you've mentioned that in May, when you were sent to Bosnia, that you were supposed to meet with Ratko Mladic. Did you know Ratko Mladic before May of 1992? And, if so, how did you know him?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have known Ratko Mladic since April 1981. We met at the Titov Veles garrison when I served as an operative in the motorised brigade. He was the training clerk in the command of the 3rd Military District, and he came to conduct an inspection in my brigade. I was assigned to escort him on that day. We did not get along well the day we met; however, we cooperated well afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in 1992, in May, when you arrived in Han -- I'm sorry, I can't pronounce the name. When you arrived, you said you met with Ratko Mladic and he told you that the Serb Republic of Bosnia was going to have its own army. Did you decide to join that army?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That army which eventually came to be known as the VRS. What position did you hold, and what was your rank?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I arrived there in the rank of Major-General. I was Chief of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska and, at the same time, deputy commander of the Main Staff, that is to say, Mladic's deputy. I was promoted to Colonel General on the 28th of June, 1994, and I was promoted to the rank of Colonel General as minister of defence, I think in 1999. Also on the 28th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you tell us what the abbreviation or the acronym is in Serbian for the position of Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: NGS, or "Sh" in B/C/S. And in abbreviated form it was "N Sh," Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And how long did you work in that position as Chief of Staff for General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: From the 11th of May until the 23rd of December. From the 11th of May, 1992, until the 23rd of December, 1996. However, I remained at the location of the Main Staff until the 27th of April, 1997, when we disbanded.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you tell the Judges briefly what was your role or your duties as -- as Chief of Staff vis-à-vis General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: My job was to organise the work of the staff. That is to say, that I was the head of the staff. I was the Chief of Staff. I was the first assistant of the commander in charge of military operations of the army. That is to say, that the preparations and conduct of military operations as well as planning of military operations and typically the beginning of implementation of each operations was under my jurisdiction. Later on, the conduct of the operation could have been assigned to another person, or the commander could have left it under my command. That is to say, that I was in charge of the practical use of the Army of Republika Srpska. In addition to me, he also had six other assistants: For morale, for logistic, security, finance, chief of air force administration. I don't know if I skipped anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's fine for my purposes today. You mentioned earlier the Main Staff. I think I have also seen in documents and heard the terms, General Staff; sometimes Supreme Command Staff. Can you tell us what the differences are between those three terms in regards to the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: When an armed conflict erupts, regardless of who the opponent is, whether the opponent is a foreign occupying force or it transpires in a civil war, as was the case in Bosnia and Herzegovina, a state that is not entirely properly organised can only be proclaimed by means of the constitution but does not have all elements of statehood - military, police, and judiciary. Republika Srpska was proclaimed on the 9th of January, 1992. It had its constitution but not its own army. In such cases, military leadership is established and is known as the Main Staff. They function as the Main Staff up until the state is completely legally properly organised, at which point it is transformed into General Staff. All countries have General Staffs in peacetime. All countries that are recognised as independent countries. During wartime, General Staff is -- is transformed into the Staff of Supreme Command. Our Staff of the Supreme Command was to be transformed into the General Staff or during the war it was supposed to be known as the Supreme Command Staff, as the Muslims had. However, we couldn't have it for two main reasons. The first reason is that the newly established command that was established in early December of 1992, the commander of the Main Staff -- or General Staff was not included, who was supposed to become a member of the command as chief of the General Staff. In this case, this was General Ratko Mladic. So we remained as Main Staff. That is to say, we were neither General Staff or Supreme Command Staff. That is the genesis -- rather, these are the origins of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation. In 1992, your staff consisted of approximately how many people, how many generals, on the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the VRS on the 12th of May when the assembly adopted the decision to establish the VRS, there were five of us generals from the JNA. Ratko Mladic, General Gvero, General Djukic, I, and General Talic, who, until that time, was commander of the 5th Corps of the JNA, which was later renamed the 1st Krajina Corps of the VRS. There were five generals, including me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And by December of 1992, what was the makeup or the size of the Main Staff of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Main Staff was established on the eve of the Assembly session of the 12th of May. There were 12 of us on the staff. Four generals, the ones I mentioned, except for Talic. Then there were six colonels and lieutenant-colonels. And two lower-ranking officers. That is, one lower-ranking officer, Captain Pecanac, Miodrag was his first name, who was chief of security of the commander of the Main Staff who was -- and that was Ratko Mladic. And there was an NCO who was soon promoted to the rank of lieutenant, Dusan Todic [as interpreted], who became chief of the security detail of the chief of General Staff on the Main Staff, which is me. May I mention the site where this took place?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking because you failed to mention the site a minute ago, so I thought it may be confidential. It was Crna Rijeka, 9 kilometres southeast of Han Pijesak. After that, the Main Staff was manned additionally, especially after the withdrawal of the JNA, because in these eight days until the withdrawal of the JNA we hired some officers from the command of the 2nd Military District and then we continued to man the Main Staff with our own personnel. However, the manning level never exceeded 36 level -- per cent during the war. We didn't want to take out officers from the units on the front line because which wanted them to be as well manned as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is my understanding correct that in the VRS the Main Staff was the highest echelon?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was the highest command. It was a command of strategic significance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And during 1992, in your position as Chief of Staff and deputy commander, can you tell the Judges what was the nature and the frequency of your contact with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: To save space in the facilities where we were put up, General Mladic and I had a joint office, shared an office. Among other things, that we were rarely present at the same time in the Main Staff. When he was there, I wasn't, and vice versa. We had daily contact whenever General Mladic was in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I must also explain something that you asked me to but I failed to do so. The position of deputy commander. When General Mladic was not in Bosnia-Herzegovina, I automatically become commander of the army and could remain in that capacity for up to 30 days. If General Mladic fails to return within 30 days, then the Supreme Command appoints a -- appoints somebody to stand in, but he never stayed away for longer than 30 days so that the Supreme Command didn't have to intervene. And now if you could repeat the second part of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think you've answered enough for present purposes. It was about the nature and frequency of your contact with General Mladic. I wanted to ask you if during the time that you knew General Mladic from -- from 1981, and particularly during your time as Chief of Staff, did you have the opportunity to become familiar with his personal handwriting?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you've testified -- you've told us that you have testified in -- in -- in another case in this Tribunal. I think you testified most recently in April of this year. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I understand that in connection with that testimony you reviewed a number of handwritten diaries to see if you could identify the handwriting therein. And I would like to start by showing you, on the screen in a second, it's 65 ter number 3699. And this is a copy of a chart that was used in connection with your testimony earlier this year. I think it's two pages. We'll have a look at the first page. And I will ask if you can recognise it. Are you able to see it on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I can see it. It was the -- the letters were a bit small.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are you able to read it now?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And on this first page, there are five diaries, or notebooks, that you looked at and indicated that you recognise the handwriting. And recognised it as that of Ratko Mladic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It both is and is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is correct that I reviewed five notebooks of General Mladic the first time around. I didn't read them all through, but I asked for permission to read those sections of the notebooks that referred to me, where my name is mentioned or the abbreviation that refers to me, either "N Sh" or "Milovanovic." It was 14 years ago in late 1996 when I first saw Mladic write.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the interpreters ask you if you could repeat. And when you do, I wanted to ask you, you said: "It was 14 years ago in late 1996 when I first saw Mladic write," and I'm told by my language advisor that what you said was: "last saw him write." Can I confirm for me if that's correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was the last time, 14 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now I know -- well, let me ask you this: Do you recall how many notebooks or diaries in total that you've looked at in connection with your preparation to testify in that earlier case?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I looked at a total of 23 notebooks: Five in Banja Luka and 18 here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And it's my understanding that you looked at the five in Banja Luka in July of -- of 2009, when an investigator named Alistair Graham came to see you. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: That is right. His name was Graham, but that's all I know about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 2 of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You've seen on page 1 there are five notebooks. And on the second page we see an additional 13, to add up to a total of 18 on these two pages. Do you recall when you looked at this group of 18 for the first time? Was that in April of this year?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that at the bottom there should be a date, the 22nd of April or the 23rd. On the previous page, the date indicated was the 22nd of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think -- if we could go to a landscape view, I think on the far right side of the bottom we'll see it is the 22nd of April.
