I would note, Your Honours, that the English translation says 22nd of August, but I think on the original and as the General said is -- the date is the 22nd of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Also, on this second page, we see that you've written in column number 4, which it's headed: "I do not recognise the handwriting of Ratko Mladic." Could you explain that for us?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I added a handwritten comment. It is not Mladic's handwriting, and the numbers 0668-1136, -1137, -1138, -1139, -1140, -1141, -1142. I have not answered the question under column 6 because I didn't have the time to study each document. I don't know what -- what's unclear here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah, let me try and assist. I have seen the handwritten note at the bottom where you mention certain ERN - that's our acronym regarding the numbering of evidence documents - certain page numbers, and I note that all of those page numbers are within the range of the diary that is listed as number 18 on this list. However, on this page, in column 4, which is a column that says: "I do not recognise the handwriting," you put your name. When you testified in the Stanisic and Simatovic case in April, at page 4407, Mr. Groome went through with you what had happened there. Because it's my understanding that you had identified all of the 18 notebooks as containing the writing of Mr. Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder if my friend could not lead the witness. He's testifying viva voce. This is leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, he's testified under oath in the other case. It's clear to me that there's some confusion seeing this document. I'm just trying to refer to him to his previous clarification of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And, I beg your pardon, but I also understand what you failed to understand. On page 2 which we see on screen now, while I was giving evidence to the Trial Chamber I admitted that I made a mistake on page 2. I wrongly filled in columns 3 and 4. In column 3, I should have entered "Ratko Mladic"; and in column 4, "MM." I didn't look at the first page carefully where there was a heading, so I got it mixed up. And what -- but my handwritten remark below which reads: "It is not Mladic's handwriting," this refers to the pages where the handwriting is not that of Ratko Mladic. Because you or somebody here marked each page with a number. And in the diaries, we found somebody else's handwriting on several pages of Mladic's diary. Mladic obviously consulted somebody else present. And since he had no slip of paper at hand, which was his way of communicating with me, by writing on a slip of paper, write to me what you think about it, and I couldn't answer him aloud in the meeting. But in some cases there were no slips of paper at hand, and then he would write it in his -- in his notebook and give it to his assistant whom he asked for his opinion. All the notebooks have been identified, generally speaking, as Mladic's handwriting, with the exception of the -- these numbers stated here, and I believe they refer to pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. That's what I understood, was that those seven pages listed to the bottom were the only pages in the 18 diaries that were not Mladic's handwriting, based on your review.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It can be put that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to ask about the general practice in the VRS, and I guess, before that, in -- in the JNA. Was it standard practice for yourself or for high-ranking officers to keep notebooks?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: We were made to do so, or taught to do so, at military schools. We had to follow the lectures of our teachers and make notes. That was useful for us because when we are preparing for the examinations, we had sort of shorthand textbooks, and it became the -- a habit for all of us to make notes when somebody is speaking. There was a system in the JNA to supply each officer with a so-called work book. There were two kinds: One was of a smaller format that fit in your pocket and you can use it in the field, and the other was a bit bigger and was mostly used to take notes during meetings where there's a table, at commands and staffs and so on, a table and chairs. Most all of us worked that way. We were issued these notebooks. And once they were full, we were obliged to return them. If the head of office did about his job conscientiously, he would ask them back and issue us a new one in return. But it wasn't always done. However, the principle was that you can't get a new one before you return your old one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was the standard practice, your practice, in terms of writing in the book? Is that something that did you on a dial basis, once a month, once a week?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm really sorry to interrupt. It's just the part of the witness's answer was not recorded, and I think it's important. He was saying something about the archiving of these work books.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May I inquire was that after his last recorded answer about you can't get a new one before you return your old one? General, I think the interpreters didn't catch the last part of your answer where you told us you couldn't get a new one before you returned your old one. What happened when you returned your old one? Can you tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was like this: Lower-ranking officers couldn't get a new notebook before they returned their old one which was full. However, high-ranking officers were commanders already, and then the NCO who issued work books didn't dare oppose a request from that high-ranking officer to be issued a new work -- a new notebook. So when I came there as a commander, he would certainly issue me a notebook without asking questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I assume that the case would be the same for General Mladic. If he wanted a new notebook before turning in an old one, he would get it.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: During the war we were not obliged to return the old notebooks. We used the ones that we had brought from the JNA or then we would make do with the notebooks or diaries from companies and enterprises. And there are several notes that Mladic made that were not in the standard JNA notebooks. I believe that there are note pads of the petrol industry of Serbia, which we received from the director of that company because they were friends, and the like. So that we didn't have to return our notebooks because we hadn't received them from the army in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll come to -- I think, one of those later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Before I get too far, Your Honour, I wanted to tender 65 ter 3699.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, it is admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1750, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. In 1992, while you were working as Chief of Staff, did you observe General Mladic writing in one of these diaries or notebooks or work book, however you called it?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I saw him write. But I cannot say that on this day he wrote in a standard format notebook, and on another day on a note pad of a different type. But I know that he had several notebooks. One he would carry around with him, another that would remain in the staff. It was -- it depended on the occasion, whom he was supposed to meet and where. However, each of his working day during the war was full, but not necessarily -- but that doesn't mean necessarily that there were entries for every day, because on -- there may have been days when he didn't have any meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In your experience, how frequently did you see him writing in his work book or notebook?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Every day when were at a meeting together.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think we'll see it in one of the notebooks later on there's -- sometimes there is a page or a couple of pages where a meeting appears to be recorded. There's a date and then notes. And there are two or sometimes three different colour of ink on the same page. Red and blue; or red, blue, and black. Can you explain that for us?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Let me first say that the Main Staff, in its original composition, existed for 1687 days. Whenever I was with Mladic, on any one of these days, he was writing something. Red, blue, and black ink. On one occasion, a retired colonel who was born at Romanija, Tomo Mijatovic came to visit us. He would supply us with note pads, paper, felt-tip pens, pencils, and whatever stationary material we needed for the staff and didn't have it. He organised some pensioners in Belgrade to buy that for us. On one occasion he brought us, among others, these pens that -- three-colour pens - red, blue, and black multi-colour pens. So press down one button then you write with blue ink or press another -- down another button, then it would be black ink, and so on. I didn't use them because they were clumsy to use. You press the wrong button and then your note is in red ink and you don't want it. I remember that he wrote the headings at the beginning of each meeting with red ink, and he would continue to make notes in blue or black. Or when there was an important personality, such as Lord Owen, then he would write down his naming in red ink and continue writing in blue. Or maybe if the supreme commander was present and spoke. So he used different colours to indicate the importance of the various persons who spoke. So it isn't a code or anything. He just wanted to highlight things. When he used regular pens to write and wanted to highlight something, he would put an asterisk. And he did that in texts when he prepared in advance what he should say at an upcoming meeting. Or if during the meeting he considered something especially important which could become a task for the military, he would mark that with an asterisk as well. And it was my conclusion that whenever an asterisk was at the beginning of any section of text, that was a reminder for him what to say at the meeting. And if the asterisk was embedded in the text, then it marked a section of text that he considered especially important.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like to show you a portion from one of the diaries and notebooks you've looked at.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is 65 ter 3581. And if we could put up page 1 of the B/C/S in e-court and page 7 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to ask you, to your experience --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm wondering if there's a connection between the document we see, the B/C/S, and the documents that were shown to the General on the 22nd of April, 2010. I note that the ERN is different.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is indeed item number 4 on the chart in Exhibit P1750. The difference in the ERN is -- you will see the English ERN is the same number as the B/C/S ERN that's on the chart. The J000 ERN is reference to a colour scan that was made of the document. The first time the document was scanned, it was scanned in black and white. And then a colour scan was made --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't think we have evidence of that. We have Mr. Hannis's representation; we have evidence that item number 4 in the chart is a different ERN; and now on the screen we have a -- a different ERN than the document that was shown to the witness last April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Isn't Mr. Hannis entitled to give that explanation. This isn't the type of information which the witness can testify to, is it, Mr. O'Sullivan?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, this is -- this is the difficulty. We had requested to have investigator Tomasz Blaszczyk testify regarding the -- the chain of custody, how these documents were seized by the Serbian authorities and came into our possession, but he would also testify about some of those things, about some markings that are on the documents, in terms of ERN numbers, handwritten page numbers that were put on there by someone. But Your Honours decided when we sought to add him as a witness that we didn't need him. Now, if the Defence is going to challenge based on those kind of things either I would request that you allow me as an officer of the court to indicate to you what the testimony of Mr. Blaszczyk has been under oath in another case, or allow us to call him to testify to those things. But it's clearly a procedural, logistical, technical matter. This is the original. This is a colour scan of the document that is item number 4 on the list that you looked at before. And I can simply ask him if he can look at this page and tell us if he recognises the writing on the B/C/S page that's on the screen in front of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan, unless I'm wholly missing something, with respect, I don't understand the basis of your objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: If I'm understanding Mr. Hannis, he has made the assertion that this is a document that this witness has previously looked at. And based on Exhibit P1750, that's not apparent. Now if he can establish that he has seen this document before, that may be different. But so far, that hasn't been established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Foundation, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, he has seen this document in black and white --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, could you look at the page in Cyrillic that's on the page in front of you. Do you recognise the handwriting on that document?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Although this document in front of me has nothing to do with me, I can recognise the handwriting. This is Mladic's handwriting. Especially since I know that on this date he became the commander of the Knin Corps, which is what he wrote down here. And he also added in his particular style: "Another complex and difficult task."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you say "in his particular style," what are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I am referring to this sentence: "Another complex and difficult task." Or one more complex and difficult task. Because in the previous year, 1991, he suffered a number of such difficult tasks in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... thank you. I would also like to show --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I would also like you to take a look at another page from this notebook which covers the time-period from 31 December 1991 through 14 February 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could have page number 111 in e-court of the B/C/S, and page 117 of the English. If we could scroll to the bottom of the page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, you will see a reference to a meeting from 1700 to 1800 hours. Do you know anything about that individual named there?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Meeting with Marrack Goulding, emissary from the General Secretary of the United Nations. I heard of this Goulding, but I don't know anything about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to show you now Exhibit 65 ter 10595. And, Your Honours, in light of his identification of the handwriting, I would like to tender 65 ter 3581.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: We object, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: On what basis, Mr. O'Sullivan, beyond the objection that was a part of the Defence's response which has been incorporated in the -- which has been disposed of in the Chamber's ruling?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The -- the discrepancy between the two versions. The one that the witness -- the ERN range that he said he looked at in April is different than what's on the screen now. And he's only looked at the first page of the document with the ERN number J00. So we say there's no basis here to admit this entire document. He's identified the first page of the document he's seeing now, but he hasn't looked through this entire document and said that it's what it purports to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. O'Sullivan. Mr. Hannis, what is your application?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, my application is to admit the entire document. We have disclosed to the Defence the ERN range 0668-3598 through 3695 which is item number 4 listed on the chart that the witness indicated he looked through. That is the black and white scan of the identical document that is a colour scan here. And the English version has this same ERN range 0668-3598 through 3695 with the ET designator, identifying it as an English translation. So it's the identical translation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I appreciate, Mr. Hannis, that it is necessary for you to thread your way carefully between yourself giving evidence on the one hand and the explanation such as the -- we -- we dealt with when Mr. O'Sullivan made his last objection. But do I understand your response to be that, to use the common expression of connecting all the dots, that the witness has testified that he has had an opportunity to compare the entirety of the document which you are now seeking to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can't stand here and tell you that he has looked at colour page 1 through 400 and compared to black and white page of 1 through 400 of this document. And if I need to go through and show him each page of this document, I'm going to have to request a lot more than three hours to do it, because I have 11 or 12 notebooks I want to show him. Your Honours, I would tender the whole thing in. Your Honours can look at it as easily as anybody else in the courtroom and judge for yourself whether it appears that it was all written by the same person. I think those arguments go to weight and not admissibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, would it be a solution, in order to get around the objection from the Defence, simply to show the witness the black versions which the witness has seen and -- I mean, I realize that the blue version is nicer to look at, perhaps, but if --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... for the Defence, then let's work to with the black.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I thought I would get an objection to not using the originals if I used a black and white copy because you've already heard there was instances where he wrote in three different colours on the same page. So I thought it was important to have the colour version so you could see him highlighting or underlining in red in some places and writing in blue or black in others. It's the identical document, Your Honour. The problem could be solved by your ruling in my favour and admitting the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Hannis always provides practical solutions. I appreciate that one. At the risk of my giving evidence, I submit that the documents with the ERN beginning J000, the one that was on the screen, is not identical to the ERN beginning 0668, which the Prosecutor chose to show the witness in April of last year and which is reflected in the Exhibit P1750, which is my point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It is time for the break. Mercifully. And we will consider this over the break and seek to come back with a ruling at 5.40.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: While the witness is on his way back to the stand, we considered the issues canvassed during the break. And to put it in its simplest form, there is no really issue in the Chamber's view as to the admissibility, in essence, of the document in question. The problem, as we understand it, is that, as Mr. O'Sullivan has alerted the Chamber, there may be a discrepancy between the colour scan of the original and the monochromatic scan to which the witness would have been referred in his earlier testimony. This requires the Prosecution, who is seeking to tender the document, to satisfy the Chamber as to the accuracy of the intended exhibit. And, therefore, we will mark both copies, both versions, that is, the colour version and the monochrome version, for identification. And when we would have heard submissions, when counsel would have had an opportunity to look at it again, as to which should be de-MFI'd, it will be done at that stage, and then we will have the accurate version as the exhibit. Yes, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, therefore, the colour version and the black and white version will become Exhibit P1751 and Exhibit P1752, both marked for identification. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis, before you continue, could you break at five minutes before the time of the adjournment so that we can deliver a brief oral ruling. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I'd shown you an entry in the diary where there was a person named Marrack Goulding?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. O'Sullivan, you had something ...

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I have an objection to the use to 65 ter 10595, which is on the screen. This exhibit, this document, was not on the 65 ter exhibit list. It had not -- it has not been previously disclosed to the accused. I think yesterday in your oral ruling you drew the line in the sand on the issue of due diligence on the Prosecution not being timely in its disclosure and being diligent in its approach to these matters. We submit that this 65 ter 10595 cannot be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I wasn't here yesterday when the oral ruling was delivered. But I had read it and I did want to make one remark. I was concerned about the Trial Chamber's view that we had not acted with due diligence. What had happened was our initial application was to have this witness called pursuant to 92 bis and Mr. Blaszczyk as a 92 bis -- or 92 ter as well. Trial Chamber issued its decision, I think, about ten days ago - I don't have the specific date in front of me - where you decided that we would not be allowed to call Mr. Blaszczyk and that we could call this witness but we needed to call him live rather than 92 bis. If he was going to be 92 bis, there were certain documents that we anticipated coming in from his prior testimony and his statement. Now that we have to call him live and the challenge is alive to the authenticity of these documents, we thought we could bolster the evidence by showing documents that reflect the entries in the diaries indeed did take place. That there were meetings, that there were reports made of those meetings, that certain persons were in certain places at certain times as recorded in the diary. That was the reason for our request. I understand that you may have decided it was too late, but our position is we didn't know it was going to be necessary to do that when we thought and hoped that your decision would be for this witness to be a 92 bis witness and Mr. Blaszczyk to be a 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's not on our -- it was not on our 65 ter list, Your Honour. We put it on our list of documents to show the witness, with the idea that we were trying to corroborate an entry in the diary by showing him that document but not moving to admit the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, the procedural background, so to say, that you are giving is a little bit more complex. You first asked -- OTP first asked to -- made an application for 92 bis for the witness. We decided to call him viva voce weeks ago, not ten days ago, or a few days ago. You -- after that, after we viva voce'd him, I think, a month ago or more than a month ago, you asked recently to 92 bis him -- to 92 ter him, to call him under 92 ter, and that's what we refused a few days ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I trust that you have it correct and I have it wrong. I don't have in front of me, but I have no reason --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... and that's -- and that's the reason -- that's the reason for the ruling we gave yesterday, if I'm correct, that it was yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I know, Your Honour, part of the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So there's no difficulty with the Prosecution using the document, but it can't be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan, the -- do we understand that although the disclosure was, in your view, late, it has been disclosed?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, it was uploaded yesterday, I believe, when we received the documents that were going to be used with this witness. We received it either yesterday or today. And, Your Honours, the fact that he was a 92 bis or ter doesn't support the Prosecution's submission, because they would have provided a package then. And there was no -- these documents, this particular document was not on any previous bis or ter package.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: This is a remedy which the -- which may be open, if absolutely necessary to the Defence, to remedy any prejudice that they would have suffered by the late disclosure of the intention of the Prosecution to show this document to the witness. But at this point, the point where we are in the trial, the document may be shown to the witness. But as I said earlier, it certainly could not be admitted as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I did want to indicate one more thing with regard to the issue of our diligence or lack of. You will recall an earlier decision about these diaries and the -- what would happen with this witness, and -- I don't have the exact ruling in front of me but Your Honours had indicated that if there were public testimony about the authenticity of the documents or the handwriting, then you would make a decision in light of that. There had been testimony in private session that did not get released until some time very recently. And when we did that, we thought it would not be necessary to have this witness come live or even 92 ter but as 92 bis. But even though there has been live testimony in the Tribunal here, Your Honours decided to have him come here live, and here he is. So that's all I wanted to say about that. Could we show the witness 65 ter 10595.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, you see on your screen a document dated the 28th of January, 1992. Can you tell us what kind of document this is?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a report of General Mladic, I believe, because I cannot see the signature, but I can see in the letterhead the 9th Corps command. It's a report of the corps commander to the command of the 2nd Military District of which the corps was probably part, about political talks of the president of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina, Milan Babic, and this Mr. Goulding who has recently been mentioned. Mladic reports to his --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Hannis, please phrase a question to the witness so that we don't end up having the witness indirectly put into evidence the contents of the document that you can't put in directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I'll stop him there. That's -- that's all I wanted to indicate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That there was this document and it's dated 28th and it refers to a meeting on what date? With Mr. Goulding.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The 27th of January, which is the day before the date mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all I wanted to ask about that. I'd like to move on now to tab 4, which is 65 ter number 3582.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could start by showing the witness page 1 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I see in front of me, labelled 39, I see the cover of the regular work book that was used by the JNA. And I believe this is a pocket format work book.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the words at the bottom, what does that mean: "Radna beleznica"? Pardon me pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Every institution in a society, including the JNA, have their own note pads or notebooks where records are kept of some -- records are kept of something. It's kept on a desk at the workplace or wherever, and people write in it about things that must be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And is this the type of book that you told us about earlier in your testimony that was used by yourself and other high-ranking officers in the VRS during 1992?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And actually had been used by you and other officers in the JNA before you switched to the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, if we could go to page 306 in the B/C/S in e-court, or -- and 361 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: First of all, General, do you recognise the handwriting on that page?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's the handwriting of General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And we see this is about the Session of the SRBH Assembly on the 12th of May, 1992, in Banja Luka. Do you know whether General Mladic attended that session?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The newly established Main Staff was represented by General Mladic and his assistants, but not me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... were you aware --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you aware before the 12th of May that General Mladic was going to attend that session?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I found out in -- at night, from the 11th to the 12th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how did you find out, and what did you do in connection with that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I've already said that on the 11th of May, in the afternoon, 12 of us gathered, and Mladic first informed us that on the following day the Assembly of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina would sit and probably the decision on the establishment of the Army of Republika Srpska would be taken. And that night, the 12 of us discussed what that army must do. We formulated 21 principles about the functioning of the future army. We couldn't -- they can't be called rules because we didn't know who the commander would be. We assumed it would be General Mladic. Tolimir, Gvero, Djukic flew from Han Pijesak to Banja Luka by helicopter on the following day. And I believe that this is Mladic's note from that Assembly session. He must have known about the Assembly session earlier, from before that night, and he made speaking notes for himself so -- to remind him what he should say here. And what we see here is the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender 3582.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The same objection as to the previous document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And our previous ruling applies here.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will be become Exhibit P1753, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, were we giving two numbers, one for colour and one for black and white?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Additional number, Your Honours, will be P1754. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we have an indication as to which is which, or are we always going to do colour first and black and white second or vice versa?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Colour first.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me -- I would like now to show you -- I'd like now to show you exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether it would be useful to have the ERN number of the black and white version on the screen -- on the -- on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may be -- it may be easiest -- I mean, I can read it out, but it will be the -- it will be the ERN that's listed on my use of -- documents to be used with the witness under the English ERN. Just take off the ET.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay? Thank you. Could we show the witness 65 ter 2324.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, this is a video I want to show you just briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I would indicate, with regard to this Assembly session, that you already have in evidence documents P74 and P1318.18 reflecting such a session on such a date at that location.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm just going play a couple of seconds, and I want to ask you if you recognise who's pictured sitting at the table.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recognise those gentleman on the front row?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could pause it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recognise the one on the right. The second from the right is General Momir Talic. The third from the right is General Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could forward just a bit and pause there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You see what General Mladic has in front of him. Can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: A work book, a large-format work book.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, that video --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry. That video is Exhibit P1295.15 in evidence, but I would also like to have a still photo, which has been marked as 65 ter 2324.1, tendered at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, we don't see the utility of marking this still from this video separately, because it doesn't advance anything beyond what is in the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may make a submission. It's just simply -- and maybe I should ask the witness to take his headphones off. Sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's the Prosecution's position that the notebook that he has in front of him at the Assembly is the one that is in evidence here. You will see the approximate location of where it's opened to, and when you see the real notebook, we'll ask you to make a comparison and draw a conclusion based on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: How is that -- sorry. Isn't that a leap from -- from this photograph, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't believe so, Your Honour. I'll -- I would prefer to save my submissions for the end of the case, but I'm certainly willing to make them now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, the witness wasn't present at this meeting, and so as much as we see General Mladic with a book in front of him that may look like the notebook, there is no way in which we can see that. It might as well be an army manual or something else. I mean, so, I think that other than what --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, you heard the witness testify that the book was written -- it's General Mladic's writing, that what is written on that date, the 12th of May, for the Banja Luka Assembly session is what appears to be speaking points for the General. We know from the minutes in the transcript of the Assembly session that General Mladic spoke at some length. We will, at the end of the case, ask you to compare what's in the -- the diary, what he wrote regarding speaking points and what he actually said as recorded in the Assembly and, with this picture, perhaps reach a not illogical conclusion that that, indeed, is the very same diary that we have here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We've heard you, Mr. Hannis, and in the Chamber's view this should not -- this still should not be separately admitted as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. Thank you. Next I would like to show the witness 65 ter 3583.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I guess the witness should be instructed to put his earphones on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you -- thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, next I want to show you a document that's 65 ter number 3583.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And could we start by showing the witness the cover page in the B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You see that, General? Is that the same type of JNA work book that we've been talking about and looked at before?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go to page 123 of the B/C/S in e-court and page 124 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recognise the handwriting on that page?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's Mladic's.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And the bottom half of that page refers to a meeting in Pale on the 9th of June with the Presidency, apparently attended by Mladic, Gvero, and Tolimir. Did you know about that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I probably did. But somebody had to stay at the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would indicate for the Court that Exhibit P260 in evidence is a document reflecting a meeting of the Presidency on that date. And I would like to tender 3583. Before I do, I should indicate, Your Honour, that with the Witness ST-215 some time ago I introduced an excerpt from this diary. I think it's page numbers -- page numbers 246 to 272 of the English regarding a meeting in Zvornik on the 30th of June, and it was admitted as an MFI at the time. What I want to do is put in the whole diary that covers the time-period from the 27th of May to the 31st of July, 1992. So I don't know what your preference would be, whether to give this that same number and take an MFI on and have the whole document in or if you want to give this a new number. I guess, since it's going to be MFI for colour and black and white, we should give it two numbers, one for colour and one for the black and white.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You're suggesting the old MFI number?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if that's more convenient or confusing for the Court. I hate to lose the old number because that was discussed with Witness ST-215 and there are references to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We're advised by the Registrar that the simpler course would be just to issue two new numbers. If anything, the old MFI number would be overtaken and would fall away eventually.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, therefore the colour version is Exhibit P1755 and the black and white one is P1756, both marked for identification. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. One follow-up point concerning this meeting. If we could show the witness page 126 -- I'm sorry. It's -- it would be page 125 for the witness in B/C/S and 126 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: There's a reference to presidential decrees for three individuals at the bottom of the page. Can you tell us anything about that? Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was requested that presidential decrees for General Grubac, I can't read the second name, and for Sipcic not be drafted. I remember that. Mladic issued me the order over the phone on the same day from Pale, because the Ministry of Defence of the RS didn't have the capabilities to provide supply to the army and to do administration work, and that's why we drafted the presidential decrees in the Main Staff and sent them to Karadzic to sign them. And I remember this because I was against appointing Sipcic corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. General, if we could go next to page 373 in the B/C/S, in e-court, and 373 in the English as well. Again, this is from the same notebook, General. And it reflects a meeting on the 27th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm not sure I have the right B/C/S page. Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 371.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. Do you recall this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was present, although Mladic didn't -- doesn't mention me. It was a meeting with the Ministry of the Interior, Mr. Mico Stanisic, and the deputy prime minister in charge of interior policies, and that was Mr. Milan Trbojevic. The two of us represented the cabinet; and Mladic, Tolimir, and I represented the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In the interests of time, I want to move on to tab 11, which is 65 ter 3584. I don't know if I indicated to Your Honours that P260 is a reflection of that earlier June 9th meeting. And if we could start by showing the witness page 23 of the B/C/S. It's page 16 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recognise the handwriting on that page, General?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's Mladic's.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And it's recording a meeting on the 2nd of August, 1992, with the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we could go next to 65 ter 1246. This is, again, a document that was not on our 65 ter list, but I'm showing it for the purposes of trying to authenticate this particular diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Perhaps I'm missing something, but the previous one, tab -- tab 11, is not tendered yet; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hadn't asked to have it tendered yet because this document relates to a meeting referred to. The next document that I had asked to be called up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... okay. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- refers to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, do you see that document refers to minutes of a meeting of the Presidency on the 2nd of August?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I can see the introductory part, and it matches the list of persons present in Mladic's handwriting; whereas, I'm unfamiliar with the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And in this document -- I'm sorry, back to the notebook. I wanted to ask you about a certain portion at page 89 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I believe it's at page 23 of the English. That's in 65 ter 3584, tab 11. [Microphone not activated] General --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: On your screen you have a document that shows a conversation occurring on the 20th of August, 1992. Do you recognise the writing on that page?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm sorry -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mladic's.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we have the wrong page in English. I think I need page 82; I misspoke. And it's about a conversation with officers from the BiH in the 2nd and 3rd armies. If we could go to the next page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall having looked at this during proofing and noted the difference in the writing on this page from the last page?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I remember this document. This is not Mladic's handwriting. This is the handwriting of Captain Pecanac, as Mladic noted at the end of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go forward to page 93 of the B/C/S in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I ask why? If there's been changes to or additional evidence that's just come up right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Because it came up about an hour before we started the session today.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, General, can you tell us about the handwriting on this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I mean, I don't think the disclosure of a proofing note is contingent on when the proofing took place. I submit we're entitled to a proofing note if there is, as we've just seen, some substance to what was discussed during proofing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this witness is being called for the limited purpose of authenticating a document. utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I was going ask, Mr. O'Sullivan, where is -- we've heard your intervention, but what is your -- where are you inviting the Chamber to go?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, can you -- we've heard you about the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: There is not a note from the proofing and there was not a note taken of this. There was a green or a red sticky put on that page in the diary. That's the proofing note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Was there any proofing? And when did it take place?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Pardon me, Your Honour? I didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Sorry. We should not overlap.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I see it now on the transcript. [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: My question was --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Please do not overlap. My question was if there was a proofing and when it took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had some proofing with the witness yesterday. And this morning Mr. Krgovic met with him briefly, and I spoke with him for about 20 minutes after that meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And we are to understand that no notes were taken from any of these proofing sessions that you had with the witness. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This particular note was as a result of my finding what appeared to be different handwriting and asking the witness about it after our meeting with Mr. Krgovic this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, what can you tell us about the handwriting on this page?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. It appears that there are two different writings on this page. What can you tell us about them?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. From the top of the page onwards, we see the handwriting of Captain Pecanac. And then at the bottom, in order to disassociate himself from it, Mladic wrote: "The above was written by Captain Pecanac." That is written by Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm really -- I'm really sorry. I didn't want to ... it's just the part of the answer which might be important was not recorded. The witness was talking something about the time when General Mladic wrote this at the end of this page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... could the witness repeat his answer, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honours. It wasn't turned on, so the interpreters cannot hear your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry. I was asking the witness -- thank you, Mr. Krgovic. I was inviting the witness to repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the bottom it says, it is written in Mladic's handwriting: "The above was written by Captain Pecanac." Which means that Mladic wrote it upon seeing the notes above. It seems to me as though he had a premonition that these notes would eventually end up here, so he wanted to disassociated himself in advance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't have any other questions about that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to tender 3584.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan, the same objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, I didn't rise because I thought there was -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I have a question in that regard. So your position is that all these different -- well, the scans of all these different notebooks, there is a discrepancy in all the scan -- in the scans of all these notebooks; right? In between the coloured one and the black and white one. That's why we're doing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can you give us an idea about what the nature is of the discrepancy?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That might be best left for me to explore that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the colour version will become Exhibit P1758, and the black and white one -- yes, P1757, thank you, Your Honour. And the black and white one P1758, both marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could turn now to P -- I'm sorry, 65 ter 3585. And I'd like to start out by showing the witness page 41 of the B/C/S in e-court. And if we could have page 33 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, do you recognise the handwriting on that page of the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... at the bottom --

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mladic's handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... thank you. And at the bottom we see a reference to the EC team and the leader Mayhew. Do you know what that team was or who that was?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At the top of the page you see a reference to General Lisica. Lisica. Do you know who he was?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It says Colonel Lisica. He was a neighbour of mine. We were both born in the same village. We graduated together from the school for non-commissioned officers. We served in Benkovac together and then we split. I went to the academy, and after the academy he went to Leskovac and then to Benkovac. I know the man very well. Right now he's a retired general.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know where he was deployed in 1992, September of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: He was the commander of Tactical Group 3 as is written here. He participated in combat between Derventa and Brod. At this time, as this was written, Lisica was somewhere in the environment of Brod and he entered Brod on the 7 of October, 1992, within the Operation Corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And during 1992 was he ever deployed in the area of Doboj?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was commander of the Operations Group Doboj upon entering Brod. Since the tactical group is a temporary formation, it is established only for the purposes of a certain mission. And you can see here that three brigades were within that tactical group. Once Brod was taken, that group was disbanded and a new group was established. Operations Group Doboj or Operations Group 9, and Lisica was the commander of that operations group up until August of 1993 when he became commander of the centre of military schools, whereas his successor was Colonel Arsic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I would like to tender 3585, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Does the same problem arise in this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So as before, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the colour version is Exhibit P1759, and the black and white one is P1760, both marked for identification. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, I have, perhaps, a slight problem with the English ERN number. There's no ET.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Hmm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Should there be one for the colour version?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I have just a moment. I think there should. This document was item number 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, item number 8 on the list of documents that the witness reviewed, and its -- its B/C/S ERN was 00 -- it was 0668-2011 through 2080, or 81 it appears. So I'm assuming the English version should be ET. That should be ET -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We are talking about tab 13 for the coloured version; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. And there in the ERN -- in the English ERN there should be ET --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- behind the coloured version.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now if we could move to tab 15. It's 65 ter number 3585.1. And first if we could show the witness the cover page in B/C/S, the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, you mentioned that sometimes General Mladic used notebooks other than that JNA one we've seen. Sorry, this is only -- this appears to be black and white. Can you recall having seen a notebook like this? I can't tell you what colour it is in real life.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mladic used up the JNA notes that he had brought with him from Knin. Later on, as the old ones were all used up, we all started using various note pads, notebooks, whatever we got. I don't remember this cover, this particular cover, but it's possible that there was one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let's -- if we could go to the next two pages in succession, I'll ask to you take a look at them and see if that helps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we have page 2 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We can see this now. Now, this is work log-book, or work diary, sort of a civilian notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And page 3. If we could enlarge the print at the bottom of the page and bring that up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is a notebook issued by a company called "Savremena izdanja, Savremena administracija," which is to say that Mladic received the notebook from this company. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No problem, General. It's happened to me before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go to page 4 of the B/C/S and page 4 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see this is recording a meeting on the 14th of September, 1992, of the 20th Session of the Assembly in Bijeljina. Do you recognise the handwriting on that page?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mladic's handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I would direct your attention to Exhibit P430 as a document in evidence recording that session of the Assembly on that date at that location. And I would move to tender 3585.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: We object to the admission of this document, and our reasons are the following: There is no colour scan of this particular document. Your Honours will have noticed that the colour scan all begin with the ERN J000, and there's no J000 version of this document. However, the version you have on the screen was not reviewed by this witness according to Exhibit P1750, which is the notes the General made of -- to 18 notebooks. I don't believe he's ever seen this particular notebook before today.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness testified before that he had seen 18 notebooks in April of this year, that he had seen another five in July of 2009 when Alistair Graham came to see him in Banja Luka. In the witness's statement, I can indicate to you that this exhibit is one of the five listed in his statement at paragraph 24 as one of the five that he reviewed in July 2009. Now my learned friend doesn't like black and white. I'm really perplexed as to what I need to provide to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1761, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And again, Your Honour, just at this point I would like to indicate to you that the explanation about why there's not a coloured scan of this one and the other four of those five shown to the witness in 2009 is something that could be explained by Mr. Blaszczyk and/or Erin Gallagher, an investigator, who dealt with these. Let me turn next to 65 ter 3585.2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, you haven't for gotten the five minutes we need.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I mean, if you can finish within four -- three minutes, all well and good.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, you may have noticed I'm running a little ragged and my voice is running out. I would appreciate if I just stop now and we dealt with your oral ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. General Milovanovic, we -- as I indicated to you, your testimony is going to extend into tomorrow. We are about to take the adjournment for today, but we have certain administrative matters with which to deal with before we rise. We are now excusing you as a witness, and the usher would escort you from the courtroom. But before he does, I would point out that you, having been sworn as a witness, you cannot have any communication with counsel from either side. And in such communications as you may have outside of the courtroom, you cannot discuss your testimony. So you are now excused until tomorrow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I'm advised that the interpreters may not have this, so I will read at dictation speed. On the 5th of November, the Zupljanin Defence orally requested the re-call of Nedjelko Djekanovic, who testified in these proceedings in October of 2009. The request arose from the subsequent testimony of ST-241, who was detained in the municipal prison at Kotor Varos in October 1992. On 5 November 2010, ST-241 testified that he was informed by his brother who was also detained in the prison that one of the men who arrived at the prison during a visit of the International Committee of the Red Cross on the 3rd of October, 1992, was the Accused Stojan Zupljanin. ST-241 testified that Djekanovic and anothers were also present. The information was not included in ST-241's Rule 65 ter summary and only became known to the Prosecution when proofing the witness prior to his appearance. Therefore, the Defence was only placed on notice of this aspect of the anticipated evidence of ST-241 shortly before he testified. The Zupljanin Defence submits that had it been aware of ST-241's description of those who were present during the ICRC visit, the Zupljanin Defence would have explored this with Djekanovic when he testified. As it was, neither the Prosecution nor the Defence raised the issue of this visit to the Kotor Varos prison with Djekanovic. Hence, the Zupljanin Defence now seeks to cross-examine Djekanovic further on the limited question of the accused's presence at the Kotor Varos prison during that visit. The Prosecution opposes the request on the basis that Djekanovic's presence at the ICRC visit was known to the Defence since early stages of the trial and is not new information for which he needs to be re-called. The evidence of ST-241 in relation to the alleged presentation of Stojan Zupljanin in the ICRC -- at the ICRC visit is new information which is directly relevant to the Defence of Stojan Zupljanin. The evidence to be elicited from Djekanovic is not cumulative in nature with other evidence on record. The Defence has, therefore, shown good cause for its request, and the Chamber finds it necessary to re-call Djekanovic for further cross-examination and re-examination, if any, on the sole issue of whether Zupljanin was present at the Kotor Varos prison on the 3rd of October, 1992, during the ICRC visit. The Chamber grants the Zupljanin Defence 30 minutes for such examination and orders that this witness may be heard after the winter recess. Thank you. So we take the adjournment to tomorrow afternoon at 2.15.
